method.prompt: If m and n are both even integers, then m + n is even.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If m and n are both odd integers, then m + n is even.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If m and n are odd integers, then mn is odd.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If n is an odd integer, then n² is odd.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If n is an even integer, then n² + n is even.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If x and y are rational numbers, then x − y is rational.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If x and y are rational numbers, then xy is rational.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If m and n are perfect squares, then mn is a perfect square.
method.why: m = k² and n = j² unpack at once; mn = (kj)² is the positive conclusion.

method.prompt: If m + n and n + p are even integers, then m + p is even.
method.why: Both hypotheses unpack (m + n = 2k, n + p = 2j); subtract and compute m + p = 2(k − j) + 2n... a positive conclusion reached directly.

method.prompt: If a, b, c are integers with a ≠ 0, a | b and b | c, then a | c.
method.why: “a | b” unpacks to b = ak; substitute into c = bj and the conclusion appears.

method.prompt: If n is an even integer, then n³ is even.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If m is even and n is odd, then m + n is odd.
method.why: Hypothesis unpacks immediately (n = 2k, x = p/q, n = k²) and the conclusion is positive: compute straight through.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd.
method.why: The hypothesis is about an expression in n, which you cannot unpack; the negated conclusion “n is even/odd” unpacks to n = 2k at once.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and n³ + 5 is odd, then n is even.
method.why: The hypothesis is about an expression in n, which you cannot unpack; the negated conclusion “n is even/odd” unpacks to n = 2k at once.

method.prompt: If m and n are integers and mn is even, then m is even or n is even.
method.why: The conclusion is an “or”; negating it gives the “and” m odd and n odd, which unpacks easily and forces mn odd.

method.prompt: If x and y are real numbers with x + y ≥ 2, then x ≥ 1 or y ≥ 1.
method.why: Negate the “or”: x < 1 and y < 1, then add the inequalities to contradict the hypothesis.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and n² is even, then n is even.
method.why: n² even does not unpack to anything about n; “n is odd” unpacks to n = 2k + 1 and squares to an odd number.

method.prompt: If n = ab with a and b positive integers, then a ≤ √n or b ≤ √n.
method.why: Negating the “or” gives a > √n and b > √n; multiply to get ab > n, contradicting n = ab.

method.prompt: If x is irrational, then 1/x is irrational.
method.why: “x is irrational” cannot be unpacked, but the negated conclusion “1/x is rational” gives 1/x = p/q, so x = q/p is rational.

method.prompt: If x is irrational, then x/2 is irrational.
method.why: Negated conclusion: x/2 = p/q is rational, so x = 2p/q is rational, contradicting the hypothesis.

method.prompt: If x, y, z are integers and x + y + z is odd, then at least one of x, y, z is odd.
method.why: Negate “at least one is odd” to “all are even”; then the sum is even.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and 5n + 3 is even, then n is odd.
method.why: The hypothesis is about an expression in n, which you cannot unpack; the negated conclusion “n is even/odd” unpacks to n = 2k at once.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and n² is odd, then n is odd.
method.why: n² odd does not unpack; “n is even” gives n = 2k and n² = 2(2k²) is even.

method.prompt: If n is an integer and n² + 1 is even, then n is odd.
method.why: The hypothesis is about an expression in n, which you cannot unpack; the negated conclusion “n is even/odd” unpacks to n = 2k at once.

method.prompt: If the product of two integers m and n is odd, then both m and n are odd.
method.why: Negate the conclusion: one of them is even, say m = 2k; then mn = 2(kn) is even.

method.prompt: √2 is irrational.
method.why: A bare negative claim (“irrational”), not an if-then: assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms and derive that p and q are both even.

method.prompt: √3 is irrational.
method.why: Bare negative claim: assume √3 = p/q reduced; 3 | p² forces 3 | p, then 3 | q, contradicting lowest terms.

method.prompt: ∛2 is irrational.
method.why: Bare negative claim: assume ∛2 = p/q reduced and use the lemma “n³ even ⇒ n even” to make both p and q even.

method.prompt: √6 is irrational.
method.why: Bare negative claim: assume √6 = p/q reduced; p² = 6q² makes p even, then q even.

method.prompt: There is no rational number r with r³ + r + 1 = 0.
method.why: “There is no …” is a negative existence claim: assume r = p/q in lowest terms and check parities of p³ + pq² + q³.

method.prompt: There are no positive integers x and y with x² + x + 1 = y².
method.why: Negative existence claim: assume a solution and squeeze y² between x² and (x + 1)².

method.prompt: log₂ 3 is irrational.
method.why: Bare negative claim: assume log₂ 3 = p/q, so 2^p = 3^q, an even number equal to an odd one.

method.prompt: There is no largest even integer.
method.why: Negative existence claim: assume a largest even integer N and produce N + 2.

method.prompt: There is no smallest positive rational number.
method.why: Negative existence claim: assume a smallest positive rational r and produce r/2.

method.prompt: If x is irrational and y is rational, then x + y is irrational.
method.why: If-then with a negative conclusion; contraposing still leaves “x is rational or y is irrational” to unpack. Assume x irrational, y rational, and x + y rational, then x = (x + y) − y is rational.

method.prompt: If x is a nonzero rational number and y is irrational, then xy is irrational.
method.why: Assume p and ¬q: xy = r rational, so y = r/x is rational, contradicting the hypothesis.

method.prompt: If n is a perfect square, then n + 2 is not a perfect square.
method.why: Negative conclusion (“not a perfect square”): assume n = k² and n + 2 = j², then (j − k)(j + k) = 2 has no integer solutions.

method.prompt: If x is irrational and x > 0, then √x is irrational.
method.why: Assume p and ¬q: √x = p/q rational, then x = p²/q² is rational, contradicting the hypothesis.

method.prompt: If a, b, c are integers with a² + b² = c², then at least one of a, b, c is even.
method.why: Assume the hypothesis and that a, b, c are all odd; then a² + b² is even but c² is odd.

method.prompt: If x is irrational and y is rational, then x − y is irrational.
method.why: Assume x − y = r rational; then x = r + y is rational, contradicting the hypothesis.

method.prompt: If x is a nonzero rational number and y is irrational, then y/x is irrational.
method.why: Assume y/x = r rational; then y = rx is rational.

method.prompt: If n is an integer, then n² − 2 is not a perfect square.
method.why: Negative conclusion: assume n² − 2 = m²; then (n − m)(n + m) = 2, impossible for integers.

method.prompt: An integer n is odd if and only if n² is odd.
method.why: “If and only if”: prove (→) directly and (←) by contraposition.

method.prompt: An integer n is even if and only if 7n + 4 is even.
method.why: “If and only if”: two directions, labeled (→) and (←).

method.prompt: For integers m and n, m² = n² if and only if m = n or m = −n.
method.why: “If and only if”: prove both directions; (→) factors (m − n)(m + n) = 0.

method.prompt: A real number x is rational if and only if 2x is rational.
method.why: “If and only if”: both directions are direct.

method.prompt: An integer n is odd if and only if n + 1 is even.
method.why: “If and only if”: two direct directions.

method.prompt: An integer n is even if and only if 3n + 2 is even.
method.why: “If and only if”: (→) direct, (←) by contraposition.

method.prompt: A real number x is rational if and only if x + 1 is rational.
method.why: “If and only if”: both directions are direct.

method.prompt: An integer n is odd if and only if n³ is odd.
method.why: “If and only if”: (→) direct, (←) by contraposition.

method.prompt: Show that for an integer n these are equivalent: (i) n is even; (ii) n − 1 is odd; (iii) n² is even.
method.why: Three statements to be shown equivalent: prove the cycle (i) → (ii) → (iii) → (i).

method.prompt: Show that for an integer x these are equivalent: (i) 3x + 2 is even; (ii) x + 5 is odd; (iii) x² is even.
method.why: “Equivalent” with three statements: prove a cycle.

method.prompt: Show that for a real number x these are equivalent: (i) x is rational; (ii) x/2 is rational; (iii) 3x − 1 is rational.
method.why: “Equivalent” with three statements: prove a cycle.

method.prompt: Show that for an integer n these four statements are equivalent: (i) n is even; (ii) n + 1 is odd; (iii) 3n + 1 is odd; (iv) 3n is even.
method.why: Four statements: one cycle of four implications covers every direction.

method.prompt: Show that for an integer n these four statements are equivalent: (i) n is odd; (ii) 5n + 6 is odd; (iii) n² is odd; (iv) n + 1 is even.
method.why: Four statements: prove (i) → (ii) → (iii) → (iv) → (i).

method.prompt: Show that for an integer n these are equivalent: (i) n is odd; (ii) n² + 1 is even; (iii) n + 2 is odd.
method.why: “Equivalent” with three statements: prove a cycle.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: the product of two irrational numbers is irrational.
method.why: Test examples first: √2 · √2 = 2 is rational, so the statement is false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: the sum of two irrational numbers is irrational.
method.why: √2 + (−√2) = 0 is rational: false, so give the counterexample.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if n is a positive integer, then n² + n + 1 is prime.
method.why: n = 4 gives 21 = 3 · 7: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: every odd integer greater than 1 is prime.
method.why: 9 is odd and not prime: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: for integers a, b, c, if a | bc then a | b.
method.why: 6 | 3 · 4 but 6 ∤ 3: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if x + y is rational, then x and y are rational.
method.why: x = √2, y = −√2 sum to 0: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: the sum of two perfect squares is a perfect square.
method.why: 1 + 1 = 2 is not a perfect square: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if n is prime, then 2ⁿ − 1 is prime.
method.why: n = 11 gives 2047 = 23 · 89: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if x is irrational, then x² is irrational.
method.why: x = √2 has x² = 2: false.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: the product of two rational numbers is rational.
method.why: Try to break it first; it holds, and rationals unpack (p/q · r/s), so prove it directly.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if x is a nonzero rational number and y is irrational, then xy is irrational.
method.why: It holds; the conclusion is negative and contraposition leaves irrationality to unpack, so assume p and ¬q.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if x is irrational, then 1/x is irrational.
method.why: It holds; the negated conclusion “1/x rational” unpacks, so contrapose.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if n is an integer and n² is even, then n is even.
method.why: It holds; “n is odd” unpacks, so contrapose.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: the sum of an even integer and an odd integer is odd.
method.why: It holds and both hypotheses unpack: 2k + (2j + 1).

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: if n is an integer and 3n + 2 is even, then n is even.
method.why: It holds; the hypothesis is an expression in n, so contrapose to “n odd ⇒ 3n + 2 odd”.

method.prompt: Prove or disprove: √5 is irrational.
method.why: It holds and is a bare negative claim: assume √5 = p/q in lowest terms.
